The online prototype extends prior agent pipelines with executable upstream requirements guards on bound requirement artifacts. The contribution is encodability and traceability of governance constraints, not causal effectiveness.

title: AI Meets Program Analysis: Lessons from a Decade of Enterprise Software Modernization at IBM
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd International Workshop on AI for Software Modernization
abstract: Generative AI has rapidly transformed software engineering through code generation, explanation, translation, documentation, and agentic development workflows. This transformation raises a fundamental question: what is the role of program analysis in the era of AI? Drawing on a decade of enterprise software modernization research at IBM, this paper argues that AI and program analysis are not competing technologies but complementary capabilities. Program analysis provides semantic evidence, dependency reasoning, correctness guarantees, and architectural constraints, while AI leverages this evidence to generate code, produce documentation, derive specifications, assist architectural design, and improve developer productivity. We illustrate this synergy through IBM's modernization research spanning legacy software understanding, business function extraction, service refactoring, APIfication, code generation, COBOL-to-Java translation, and automated testing. Across these workflows, a consistent lesson emerges: the most reliable and trustworthy AI-assisted modernization is achieved when AI is grounded in semantic artifacts extracted and validated through program analysis. Looking ahead, we envision enterprise software engineering as a collaboration in which program analysis provides evidence, AI provides intelligence, and human engineers contribute the judgment and wisdom required to build trustworthy software systems.

title: Automating Low-Risk Code Review at Meta: RADAR, Risk Calibration, and Review Efficiency
venue: Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering
abstract: AI-assisted coding tools have altered software production. At, significant lines of code per human-landed diff grew by 105.9% year over year and per-developer diff volume rose 51%, with agentic AI responsible for over 80% of that growth. Meanwhile, the share of diffs receiving timely review has declined, exposing a widening gap between code supply and reviewer bandwidth. We therefore ask three questions that progress from feasibility through calibration to impact: (1) can risk-stratified automation operate at scale across diverse organizations, (2) how does tuning the risk threshold affect the trade-off between automation yield and safety, and (3) to what extent does automated review reduce end-to-end latency for AI-generated changes? To answer them, we deployed RADAR (Risk Aware Diff Auto Review), a multi-stage funnel that classifies each diff by authorship and source type, applies eligibility gates, static heuristics, a machine-learned Diff Risk Score, LLM-based Automated Code Review, and deterministic validation before landing qualifying changes. We evaluate RADAR through telemetry covering 535K+ RADAR-reviewed diffs, observational before–after comparisons for policy changes, and difference-in-differences analysis of efficiency outcomes. RADAR has reviewed 535K+ diffs and landed 331K+. Relaxing the Diff Risk Score threshold from the 25th to the 50th percentile raised the approve rate to 60.31%. The revert rate for RADAR-reviewed diffs is 1/3 that of non-RADAR diffs, and the Production Incident () rate is 1/50 that of non-RADAR diffs. Compared to human-reviewed diffs, RADAR reduces median time to close by more than 4.3× and median diff review wall time by 35%. We conclude that risk-aware layered automation can materially reduce review bottlenecks created by AI-driven code growth without compromising production safety during incremental rollout.

title: Specifying the Delegated-Autonomy Boundary: Requirements Engineering for Agentic AI
venue: Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering
abstract: Agentic AI systems do not just predict or recommend; they plan, maintain state, and act in external environments with varying degrees of autonomy. This changes the requirements engineering problem in a specific and under-addressed way: it introduces what we call the delegated-autonomy boundary - the set of decisions about what may be delegated to the system, under what graduated authority, with what oversight, and how control is returned. Current practices bury these decisions inside prompts, tool schemas, and runtime policies, even though they are requirements-level commitments. This paper proposes two complementary artifacts. First, an Agency Justification Record (AJR) helps teams decide when an agent is warranted over simpler alternatives. Second, an Agentic Delegation Policy (ADP) captures what must be specified for safe and effective development: purpose, authority, information, coordination, assurance, and evolution. Crucially, authority in the ADP is modelled as graduated, i.e., a tiered structure. We illustrate the framework with two contrasting examples: a safety-critical hospital discharge coordination agent and an automated code review agent.

title: Evaluating the Impact of Explainable AI on Trust in AI-Assisted Code Review
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering
abstract: The use of large language models (LLMs) for automated code review has brought significant change to a time-consuming part of software engineering. Prior work has shown that LLM-based code tools can improve code quality and enable more robust software development processes. As the tools get more powerful, the explanations behind their decisions remain hard to understand. Developers struggle to assess the validity of LLM-generated code reviews, making it difficult to gauge how much trust they should place in them. While the application of automated code review with LLMs has been extensively investigated, the inclusion of Explainable AI (XAI) for transparency in code reviews and its impact on trust are yet to be explored. We aim to address this research gap by studying the influence of XAI on the trust of software developers in AI-assisted code reviews. We conducted a within-subjects user study with 34 participants from diverse programming backgrounds, comparing three experimental LLM-based automated code review systems with varying levels of XAI support: Condition A (detailed explanation and review feedback), Condition B (review feedback only), and Condition C (no explanations). Participants were shown a series of real-world code change requests along with the AI-generated code reviews. During the study, we measured trust perceptions for each system using a questionnaire, agreement with the AI recommendation, the reasoning for accepting or rejecting the code change, and the time taken to review the code change. Our quantitative results show that the level of explanation significantly influences both the level of trust of software developers and their agreement with AI recommendations, but in different ways. Full explanations (Condition A) yield the highest perceived trust (M = 3.99/5) but not the highest agreement with AI recommendations, whereas moderate explanations (Condition B) achieve the highest agreement with AI (89.22%). This could suggest that more explanations prompt developers to question AI recommendations more frequently. In contrast, providing no explanations (Condition C) results in the lowest levels of trust and agreement. We also find that the level of explanation did not significantly impact the time taken to accept or reject a code change. Across all conditions, the most commonly cited reasons for code change decisions were changes in code readability and the correctness of the implementation. Overall, these findings indicate that incorporating XAI into the code review process significantly changes the trust perceptions and agreement with AI recommendations for software developers. These results provide insights for the design and evaluation of trustworthy AI-based code review systems, and support researchers in the design of studies on the human factors of AI-assisted software development.

title: E4R-Reviewer: Effective and Explainable Automated Code Review via End-to-End Reasoning-Guided Alignment
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering
abstract: Code review is a key practice for ensuring software quality and maintainability. Despite progress in Automated Code Review (ACR), existing methods face two core challenges: (1) Isolated Task Modeling. Current approaches often model and optimize subtasks in ACR independently, ignoring the inherent logical order and internal dependencies among them which affects the effectiveness of ACR. (2) Lack of Explainability. At the task level, the absence of explanatory information in review comments increases developers’ cognitive load; at the model level, the black-box nature fundamentally undermines developer trust. To address these challenges, we propose E4R-Reviewer, which improves the E ffec­tiveness and E xplain­ability of ACR through E nd-to- E nd R easoning-guided alignment. For effectiveness , E4R-Reviewer unifies multiple fine-grained ACR subtasks into a single end-to-end reasoning process, enabling cross-task knowledge sharing and allowing the model to explicitly complete a reasoning chain that covers quality estimation, issue localization, issue classification, issue description, fix suggestion, and code refinement in one generation. Meanwhile, we adopt a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)-based reinforcement-learning alignment, treating the reasoning steps as optimizable intermediate objectives. We design subtask-specific rewards and integrate them via curriculum-inspired, multi-stage reward fusion that follows the real-world review workflow. For explainability , E4R-Reviewer produces reasoning process and structured review results covering all fine-grained ACR subtasks, improving the transparency and explainability of the review results. Extensive evaluations on public, real-world datasets demonstrate that E4R-Reviewer significantly outperforms existing methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance: a 74.61% F1-score in quality estimation and +22.96% CodeBLEU in code refinement. Furthermore, Large Language Model (LLM) and human evaluation further confirm the superiority of E4R-Reviewer in terms of effectiveness and explainability.

title: From Static to Dynamic: Benchmarking Real-World Code Review with MCR-Bench
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering
abstract: In real-world software development, code review typically involves iterative interactions between developers and reviewers to improve software quality, making the process costly and time-consuming. Although recent work explores large language models (LLMs) for automated code review, most approaches oversimplify code review into a single-round, static decision task, which fails to capture the multi-round interactive nature and the complex problem-solving processes inherent in realistic review scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce MCR-bench, the first defect state-aware benchmark designed for realistic multi-round code review. MCR-bench covers five commonly-used programming languages and consists of 2,269 real-world multi-round code review tasks, each of which is annotated with fine-grained defect information and cross-round state labels. Each task in MCR-bench is equipped with fine-grained defect metadata (e.g., description, type, severity) alongside dynamic state annotations, capturing the complete evolutionary trajectory of a defect throughout the multi-round process. We obtain several findings through extensive experiments on MCR-bench with mainstream LLMs. (1) Limited overall capability: experiments reveal that mainstream LLMs exhibit limited overall performance in defect detection and defect lifecycle state tracking, with performance degrading significantly as the number of interaction rounds increases; (2) Defect-sensitive performance: LLMs' performance varies substantially across different defect types and severity levels, with semantically complex or low-salience defects being significantly more likely to be missed; (3) Underlying Failure Mechanisms: our in-depth error analysis dissects the distinct drivers of false positives and false negatives, revealing critical weaknesses such as cross-round temporal misalignment and inadequate long-range memory.

title: Beyond Code Generation: Reassessing Software Quality in AI-Assisted Development
abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (genAI) is fundamentally transforming software engineering practices by shifting code production from deterministic, human-authored processes to AI-assisted development workflows characterised by probabilistic behaviour, prompt sensitivity, and increased process complexity. This transformation entails significant challenges for software quality evaluation, as traditional metrics, developed under the assumptions of determinism and reproducibility, are increasingly insufficient for assessing AI-assisted development. This position paper synthesises recent empirical and theoretical developments across three complementary dimensions of this transformation: the human dimension, examining the cognitive and educational implications of genAI adoption; the artefact dimension, analysing the evolution from code-centric development toward Everything-as-Code; and the technological dimension, focusing on emerging multi-agent software engineering workflows. The analysis examines how prompt sensitivity, output variability, governance challenges, and the expanding scope of Everything-as-Code practices complicate existing quality frameworks, and contends that evaluation methodologies must evolve toward process-aware, context-aware, cross-artifact, and workflow-level approaches. The educational implications of AI-assisted programming are also addressed, with particular emphasis on the lasting impact on professional software quality. This work provides a conceptual map of the changing software engineering landscape and identifies critical areas for further empirical investigation.

title: Who is in charge? Coordination and governance in agentic software engineering
venue: Journal of Logical and Algebraic Methods in Programming
abstract: AI agents are transforming software development from a human-led activity into a collaborative process involving autonomous planners, coders, testers, and reviewers. This shift raises a deceptively simple question with deep engineering and social consequences: when software work is shared between humans and autonomous agents, who is really in charge? This paper argues that the central challenge is coordination : deciding who does what, when, and under whose authority. Natural-language conversation is now the primary medium through which humans and agents interact, assign tasks, and negotiate outcomes; however, conversation is not a substitute for explicit coordination structure. We trace the evolution from Agent-Oriented Software Engineering (AOSE) to contemporary Agentic Software Engineering (ASE), and use a multi-agent code-review scenario to distinguish conversational interaction from governed coordination. The paper argues that autonomy increases the need for coordination; it does not reduce it. Making agentic systems governable therefore requires explicit mechanisms for assigning responsibility, validating outputs, escalating uncertainty, and preserving accountability. We introduce the notion of a runtime coordination contract, a lightweight governance abstraction that specifies roles, task scopes, input/output schemas, escalation conditions, and audit obligations. The paper positions coordination contracts as a runtime analogue of classical coordination and behavioral-contract mechanisms: more flexible than fully pre-designed protocols, but sufficiently explicit to support monitoring and auditability. We discuss some implications for software engineering practice. We conclude proposing an open research agenda concerning contract languages, runtime conformance monitoring, multi-agent benchmarks, and human–agent teaming.

title: The Amplifier Problem: A Constraint-Based Model of Generative-AI Impact on Software Project Delivery, with a Governance Framework for Project Managers
abstract: Generative-AI coding assistants are sold to project sponsors as schedule accelerators, yet the empirical record points in different directions. A 2023 controlled experiment reported tasks finished 55.8% faster; a 2025 randomized trial of experienced open-source developers reported tasks taking 19% longer; and the 2024 DORA survey of more than 39,000 professionals associated higher AI adoption with an estimated 1.5% fall in delivery throughput and 7.2% fall in delivery stability. These results measure different things in different populations, and none of them is a project schedule. This paper asks when a task-level AI effect becomes a project-level schedule effect. We propose the Delivery Constraint Model (DCM), which combines Amdahl’s law (coding is only one part of lead time) with a queueing model of code review (faster coding raises the arrival rate at a fixed-capacity stage). The model gives a closed-form saturation condition, a break-even map in the space of review utilization and coding speed-up, and a planning rule. A closed-form M/G/2 approximation reproduces a discrete-event simulation of 64 conditions within 0.31 percentage points on average (maximum 1.68) wherever review is not saturated. Using published effect sizes as inputs, the same tool yields a project-level change ranging from about 22% faster to about 8% slower, or an unbounded review queue, depending on the coding share of lead time, baseline review utilization and the size of AI-assisted changes. In the simulation, adding one reviewer or using a pull-based review gate keeps lead time bounded where the ungoverned system saturates; the gate costs 2% to 10% of throughput relative to the ungoverned system, and the extra reviewer raises throughput. We also define the Perception–Reality Gap (PRG), a 43-point difference between forecast and measured effect in the 2025 trial, as a risk indicator, and propose five governance controls (AADG) and a stepped-wedge validation protocol. Two real-data checks are reported. In 8,576 merged pull requests from 13 open-source repositories (191 AI-attributed), AI-attributed changes took longer to merge: 93% longer after adjustment for size, commit count, repository and quarter (95% CI +49% to +150%; randomization p < 0.002), with a positive estimate in each of the six repositories that have at least eight such changes, a pooled random-effects estimate of +60% (95% CI +23% to +108%), and no single repository driving the result (leave-one-out range +82% to +99%). Lead time is first commit to merge, not review wait, and AI use is identified only by disclosed trailers, so this is observational evidence. Published AIDev statistics (33,596 agentic pull requests) show that agents whose output relies on human review were merged less often and more slowly than human changes, and that merge rates fell for every agent in repositories with 500 or more stars. The empirical evidence is observational; confirmatory tests are left to the protocol in Section 7.

title: ReviewAnchorBench: Executable Dual-Anchor Oracles for Mapping Code Review Suggestions Across Revisions
abstract: Context: Code review suggestions bind a creation-time code range to proposed replacement text, while later commits can move, rewrite, duplicate, apply, or delete that range. Reliable longitudinal analysis therefore requires target identity, observable state, and uncertainty to be measured together. Objectives: We evaluate executable dual-anchor oracles for mapping suggested-change targets across revisions and characterize their recovery-risk trade-off. Methods: We retain a 653-anchor hard-challenge benchmark and sample 300 anchors from the source population after excluding every calibration repository. Ten deterministic transformations yield 3,790 held-out challenge cases and 3,000 population-sampled cases with exact span-and-state oracles. We compare four simple baselines, five component variants, and CodeMapper under calibration-matched location contracts. Results: The full cascade reaches 90.50% exact span-and-state recall, 1.81% localization selective risk, 1.50% negative-case false links, and 73.73% coverage in the population-sampled stratum. The corresponding hard-challenge estimates are 90.30%, 1.93%, 1.72%, and 73.67%. Removing negative guards raises population-sampled false links to 51.67%. CodeMapper's matched-risk configuration reaches 59.83% span recall at 48.43% coverage and 1.17% localization risk. Conclusion: Dual anchors improve controlled recovery across both strata, while negative guards determine whether duplicated and deleted targets produce concrete false links. The executable oracles isolate component effects and quantify the coverage cost of selective mapping. Preprint; not peer reviewed. Replication materials: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22217751

title: Test Co-Evolution and Coding-Agent Adoption in Open-Source Software Repositories
abstract: This artifact accompanies the study “Test Co-Evolution and Coding Agent Adoption” , which investigates the relationships between coding-agent adoption, production–test co-evolution, and post-adoption corrective maintenance in open-source repositories. It includes datasets covering 66 repositories, Python analysis scripts, and generated tables, figures, and statistical results. The analyses examine adoption levels, production–test co-evolution, commit-based corrective maintenance ratios (CMRpost), and issue-based corrective maintenance ratios (CIRpost). The package provides the data and derived monthly corrective-maintenance ratios needed to reproduce the final quantitative analyses without repeating the original collection pipeline. Additional scripts support repository cloning, GitHub issue collection, commit-history processing, and commit-message classification. Data, scripts, and results are distributed as ZIP archives. The README provides extraction instructions, dependency requirements, and reproduction commands. The original scripts, documentation, derived metrics, and generated results are released under the MIT License; third-party source content remains subject to applicable rights and terms.

title: Translate or Replay? Two AI-Assisted Rewrites Compared — ggblab version 1 → version 2 (n = 1) and Bun Zig → Rust: what each kept, what served as the oracle, what escaped, and what code volume measures
abstract: Technical report comparing two software rewrites carried out with AI coding agents in 2026. Bun, a JavaScript runtime, was translated from 535,496 lines of Zig into about 780,000 lines of Rust in eleven days by about 64 concurrent agents, gated by the existing test suite; the vendor reports 19 known regressions introduced by the rewrite, since fixed, four of them described (the vendor's own account, bun.com, 8 July 2026). ggblab, a GeoGebra–Jupyter bridge written for a university course, was replayed from a corrected origin along a numbered sequence of example notebooks by one agent under the author's direction between 3 and 30 September 2026; 23,331 lines of version 1 became 6,437 lines of version 2, of which 29 % are instruments (probes and tests), and an 8-gram overlap of 0.0023 between version 2's construction type and parser (330 lines) and the version-1 parser files, in the band of the negative controls, finds no verbatim overlap for this core (the measure detects token overlap, not provenance; the rest of version 2 was not measured, and one layer was carried over by design). The report names the two methods translation (structure preserved, language changed) and replay (specification preserved, structure changed) and compares them along seven axes: what is preserved, code volume, the oracle, what escaped the oracle, parallelism and time, the human's position, and reversibility. A survey with stated inclusion predicates sets the two beside thirteen other documented AI-assisted rewrites of 2024–2026 (four translations, three replays, six framework or runtime upgrades); only one of them, Ladybird's C++ to Rust port of its JavaScript front end, publishes both the size of its oracle and its regression count. Three observations follow: code volume is a dependent variable of the method and must be reported with the predicate that defines the counted set; translation keeps what the old code did silently, which is where its regressions came from, while replay does not carry the silent behaviour of the code it does not copy, and its heaviest review finding lived in the one layer it carried over and in a new adapter written for that layer; and the choice between the two is decided by whether an oracle for 'the output has not changed' exists and whether a failure is reversible. The comparison is descriptive; no ranking of the two methods is intended. The ggblab side is a single case by the author; every number is traceable to a dated record and, where it was computed, to a script named in the report. Section 2.2 defines the copy-distance measure (directed n-gram containment with a planted-derivative calibration) and gives its pseudocode. The text was reviewed against its sources by two AI reviewers of different families (Claude Opus 5.5, then GPT-6 Sol) and revised after each, then revised once more by the author, before deposit; the two reviews, the three records of changes, and the figure scripts with their outputs are deposited with the report. An AI usage disclosure is included.

title: AI Code Synthesis, Autonomous Debugging, and the Evolution of the Software Engineering Lifecycle: Repository Graph Reasoning, SWE-bench Benchmarks, and Security Bounds
abstract: Abstract — The software engineering (SWE) lifecycle has transitioned from human-centric manual programming toward autonomous AI code synthesis and closed-loop program repair. Foundation models pre-trained on billions of source code tokens—including modern frontier models and specialized coding LLMs—have evolved beyond isolated function autocompletion toward whole-repository fault localization, cross-file patch synthesis, and dynamic regression test generation. However, deploying autonomous agentic coding frameworks in enterprise software development environments exposes acute structural vulnerabilities: contextual fragmentation across massive Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs), patch-induced semantic regressions, dependency hallucination attacks (e.g., package typosquatting), and severe computational token overhead during multi-step debugging loops. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of autonomous AI code synthesis. We formalize program synthesis as directed exploration over Program Dependency Graphs (PDGs), establish the mathematical mechanics of execution-guided test-time search with verbal reinforcement feedback (Reflexion), and model repository-scale retrieval using tree-sitter AST parsing. Furthermore, we construct an empirical benchmarking testbed evaluating state-of-the-art coding architectures across 500 real-world open-source software engineering issues from SWE-bench Lite and SWE-bench Verified. Our findings demonstrate that while single-turn code generation models achieve only a 14.8% resolve rate, agentic tree-search architectures coupled with AST-guided repository graphs achieve a 46.2% issue resolution rate. Concurrently, execution-guided sandbox feedback reduces semantic patch regression by 64.8%, though AI-generated code introduces a 19.4% prevalence of unverified dependency inclusions. Finally, we formulate open research directions in neuro-symbolic program verification, verified formal specification synthesis, and automated zero-shot licensing provenance. Index Terms— AI Code Synthesis, Automated Program Repair (APR), SWE-bench, Program Dependency Graphs (PDG), Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), Repository-Level Reasoning, Software Security, Agentic Coding.

title: Optimal Context Mapping (Model D): A Permanent, Learning Map of a Repository for AI Coding Agents
abstract: Model D keeps a map of a repository on disk, so a coding agent's next session and teammates don't start from zero. Each code block and documentation sentence becomes a 1,024-bit fingerprint on the user's machine, a fixed routing law picks a short readout with no model calls, and each answered question becomes a link from that question's fingerprint to the line that answered it. This version adds the paper, which describes version 0.5.3 and reports what was measured, including the failures. In ColdSession, a pre-registered benchmark of our own on three public repositories, Model D used about half the tokens of the same agent working alone, at about the same accuracy, including after a year of real commits. It also failed the pass conditions set before the run, most of the saving comes from the map and not from memory, and on third-party benchmarks of cold search it is not ahead. The paper is licensed CC BY 4.0, and the code Apache-2.0. The four zip files unpack into one folder, holding the code and all the evidence, and SHA256SUMS lists their checksums. Source: https://github.com/devkancheti4-design/optimal-context-mapping

title: gestalt-core: local search over Markdown notes for coding agents, with a rerunnable BEIR benchmark
abstract: A Markdown knowledge base for Claude Code and Cursor, searched by stella_en_400M_v5 dense vectors in SQLite with sqlite-vec, full-text BM25 as the lexical fallback and an optional Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B rerank, plus session hooks, skills, rules and an evaluation harness. The repository reports nDCG@10 on BEIR SciFact, NFCorpus and FiQA with seeded confidence intervals and paired permutation tests, and one command reproduces the table.

title: IntentSpec: Explicit Interpretation and Independent Verification for AI-Accelerated Requirements Engineering
abstract: AI coding agents can transform software requirements into implementations rapidly, but faster implementation does not guarantee correct interpretation. Conventional natural-language requirements often leave authority, ambiguity, traceability, and verification evidence implicit, while highly formal approaches may impose substantial authoring overhead. This paper presents IntentSpec, an experimental Markdown-based requirements representation and companion agent workflow designed for joint use by human engineers and AI coding agents. IntentSpec separates normative obligations from informative context, provides stable requirement and acceptance-criterion identifiers, supports typed traceability and structural approval gates, and requires unresolved questions to remain visible. A proposed interpretation protocol asks agents to externalize triggers, obligations, constraints, assumptions, and ambiguities before implementation, while verification is treated as a separate activity requiring independent evidence rather than agent self-attestation. A working Python prototype implements structural parsing, validation, cross-reference checking, JSON export, conformance tests, and CI validation. We outline a controlled evaluation against plain Markdown, structured natural-language requirements, and an existing specification-driven agent workflow, measuring interpretation accuracy, ambiguity detection, implementation compliance, traceability, and human authoring effort.

title: When Every Agent Test Passes and the System Still Fails
abstract: Agentic software engineering can complete every assigned task while failing to deliver the enterprise outcome those tasks were intended to achieve. A dependency graph may report successful execution, individual APIs may pass their tests, and generated components may appear correct, yet the assembled system can still violate business requirements, architectural constraints, or operational expectations. This enterprise architecture whitepaper examines the gap between local agent success and system-level readiness through the context of agentic legacy migration. Drawing on an illustrative ten-API migration scenario, anonymized practitioner experience, and established systems-engineering research, it proposes a planning and verification architecture built around three responsibilities. The primary migration lane establishes known behavior, dependencies, and target capabilities before translation. A holistic verification plane compares the assembled system against approved business outcomes, intended architecture, critical journeys, cross-cutting invariants, and current runtime evidence. An exception lane classifies findings before selecting replanning, evidence acquisition, authorized decisions, or bounded remediation. A separately authorized promotion controller determines whether the evidence supports advancement of a defined migration scope. The paper introduces Migration Capsules, versioned system models, evidence freshness and invalidation controls, finding-disposition rules, residual-risk records, and five enterprise acceptance gates. It connects these proposals to established software and systems-engineering practices without claiming to introduce a new testing primitive. The proposed architecture is informed by a focused narrative review and qualitative operating experience. It is not presented as an independently validated or statistically generalizable result, and complete autonomous factory execution remains a validation objective. Intended audience: CTOs, chief architects, enterprise modernization leaders, AI engineering leaders, platform engineering teams, technology governance stakeholders, and enterprise buyers evaluating agentic software-delivery systems.

title: When Does Sub-Graph Paging Help? An Empirical Comparison of Full-Context, Top-K, Personalized PageRank, and Summary-Indexed Graph Memory for Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: I present an empirical study and reproducible in-process benchmark suite evaluating four competing retrieval paradigms for multi-agent software engineering memory under identical compact tuple serialization (25 tokens/node) across five scale tiers (20 to 800 nodes, 300 multi-hop causal path queries): Full-Context Serialization, Flat Top-K Lexical/Vector Retrieval, Budget-Matched HippoRAG (Global Personalized PageRank), and Summary-Indexed Sub-Graph Paging (both naive EngramGraph v1 and anchor-augmented EngramGraph v2). Our evaluation yields four actionable findings: 1. Small Graphs (<= 144 nodes / <= 3.6k compact tokens): Full-Context serialization achieves 100% path and node coverage with zero routing overhead; sub-graph paging is unnecessary at this scale. 2. Failure Mode of Naive Summary Paging (EngramGraph v1): Routing solely on 2-sentence sub-topic summaries degrades from 95.0% at 20 nodes to 58.3% at 384 nodes and 30.0% at 800 nodes due to summary compression loss and unmounted cross-topic bridges. 3. Structural & Anchor Mitigation (EngramGraph v2): Augmenting summary routing with an Entity-Anchor Footer (+12 tok/sub-topic), 1-Hop Bidirectional Bridge Closure, and Anchor-Seeded Subgraph Projection recovers complete-chain recall to 86.7% at 384 nodes (95.6% node coverage) and 88.3% at 800 nodes (96.1% node coverage) while reducing active prompt tokens by 77.2% to 87.7% compared to compact Full Context, and outperforming equal-budget Flat Top-K by +20.0 to +26.6 percentage points (McNemar p < 0.001). 4. Read-Only Global PPR vs. Read/Write Sub-Topic Isolation: Budget-Matched HippoRAG (Global Personalized PageRank) achieves the highest read-only recall on static graphs (98.3% at 384 nodes; 93.3% at 800 nodes), whereas EngramGraph v2 provides partitioned sub-topic write leases and Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) for concurrent multi-agent mutation workloads with zero silent lost updates.

title: Replication package: What AI Coding Agents Claim and What We Can Measure (IntentValidator, NFR claim catalog, two-rater manual validation)
abstract: Replication package for the manuscript What AI Coding Agents Claim and What We Can Measure: Non-Functional Requirement Claims, Extraction Validity, and Intent–Outcome Consistency in Agent-Authored Pull Requests , prepared for submission to Empirical Software Engineering (special issue: Agentic Software Engineering). Contents: the IntentValidator pipeline source snapshot and run configurations; the per-claim datasets of the canonical agent run, of the all-repository human comparison cohort (with its protocol, draw listings and order of events) and of the superseded first human cohort, plus the re-runs that document the effect of the pipeline's timeouts; the 186-pattern NFR claim catalog, boilerplate-stripping rules and the full match table; the extraction-validity ladder and regression scripts; the manual-validation kit (stratified samples, rubric, blind labelling tool, both human raters' sheets with untouched exports and SHA-256 sums, three disclosed LLM annotation passes with per-item rationales and provenance, the LLM-judge sensitivity, the adjudication queue, a recall probe of unflagged pull requests with blind sheets and a disclosed LLM screen, and a kit for a rater from outside the author team); the consistency analysis on the human-validated claims, the Maintainability-Index floor sensitivity and the all-language cross-check of the index against independent Halstead implementations (per-claim results); every analysis script that regenerates the manuscript's numbers and figures; and a checksum manifest of every file with named reproduction checks. The archive carries the replication tree only; the manuscript itself is not included. The AIDev dataset itself is not redistributed; obtain it from its own Zenodo record (10.5281/zenodo.16919272). The 25 September 2026 audit revision adds explicit sampling and interpretation limitations, corrected stratification of diagnostic agreement intervals, clarified nominal instrument coverage, and reproducibility notes. Original human labels and canonical claim verdicts are preserved; catalogue label/rubric conflicts remain for human reassessment. See replication/09-paper/emse-2026/replication/REVIEW-NOTES-2026-09-25.md. Version 2.0.2 (27 September 2026) follows an independent replication of version 2.0.1 from public sources only, which reproduced every result of RQ1–RQ4 and re-ran the pipeline end to end (13.1 % of evaluable agent claims consistent, as published). It adds per-PR provenance (merged flag, P2 membership, measured commits, in-scope files), extraction-tier membership and the multi-metric run's per-metric deltas, a verify mode for the checksum manifest, fixes to the AIDev download script and the manifest's date filter, and clarified requirements and licences. Released runs, labels and generated outputs are unchanged. See replication/09-paper/emse-2026/replication/REVIEW-NOTES-2026-09-27.md.

title: Outside the Prompt: Measuring Trust Boundaries of AI Coding Agents Outside the Model — Preregistration (v2)
abstract: Preregistration of the confirmatory parts of the study "Outside the Prompt", which measures where security failures of AI coding agents and their connectors trigger relative to the model's decision. It fixes, before the measurements: the research questions and hypotheses (classification of June–September 2026 disclosures with independent raters; client behaviour when an approved MCP tool definition changes; observability of these events in default host telemetry), the frozen classification criteria, the inclusion rules and neutral-summary procedure for the dataset, the raters (author and three open-weight models with exact tags and digests), the analysis plan (Cohen's and Fleiss' kappa, five repetitions per lab cell), and the lab protocols for Q3 and Q4. Measurements already run before freezing (trust boundary of repository-declared MCP servers; defence coverage in official MCP servers; a ten-case classification pilot, Fleiss' kappa 0.91) are declared as exploratory. All lab work uses systems owned by the author and harmless canaries. Target journal: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR).
